# passForElse states "the body never ran" as a flag, and sets it as the body's
# FIRST statement. That position is the whole of what makes a loop escape
# behave: `break` and `continue` both leave the rest of the body unrun, so a
# flag set anywhere after them is not set on the iteration that escaped, and
# the else fires for a loop whose body did run.
#
# This runs the generated Go rather than reading it, because the invariant is
# about order and a grep over the output is position-blind. The interpreter
# cannot see it either -- it honours For.Else natively and never runs the pass
# -- so the assertion has to come from a compiled target.
#
# The state has to be a component var. A plain function over a literal list
# const-folds before lowering, and then proves nothing about the pass.

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:ui"
import . "sngl:test"
import app "sngl:app"

component box node {
    var xs list<int> = [1, 2]
    var note = ""

    button #stop(text="stop", @click {
        for var x = xs {
            note = "saw {x}"
            break
        } else {
            note = "empty"
        }
    })
    button #skip(text="skip", @click {
        for var x = xs {
            note = "{x}"
            continue
        } else {
            note = "empty"
        }
        note = note + "!"
    })
    text(value=note)
}

// A break leaves a loop whose body ran, so the else does not run.
func testBreakMeansTheBodyRan(t Test, c box) {
    c.stop.click()
    t.assert(c.note == "saw 1")
}

// Nor does a continue on every iteration: the body ran each time, and the
// loop ended by running out rather than by never starting.
func testContinueMeansTheBodyRan(t Test, c box) {
    c.skip.click()
    t.assert(c.note == "2!")
}

app.window {
}
